Associated with stomach and intestinal dysfunction and degeneration of muscle. No fever, incoordination with diarrhea and coffee-colored urine. Affected animals are unable to stand but eat and are alert shortly before death. High blood pressure frequent. Tissue changes include heart and skeletal muscle degeneration. Congestion, fatty degeneration and tissue death in the liver and kidneys also reported. Death probably due to high blood pressure causing heart failure.; Comments and Treatment: No specific treatment known. Symptomatic and supportive care essential. Although tissue changes are similar to those of vitamin E/selenium deficiency, this therapy is contraindicated. Remove animals from source.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Fly poison, Staggergrass, Crow poison; Amianthium muscaetoxicum; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods, fields, and acid bogs; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant. Drooling, vomiting, rapid and irregular respiration, weakness, death from respiratory failure.; Comments and Treatment: No practical treatment. Especially dangerous for animals new to pasture. Keep animals well fed.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Larkspurs; Delphinium species; Habitat and Distribution: Either cultivated or wild, usually in open foothills or meadows and among aspen; mostly western. Dangerous season spring and summer, also seeds in fall.; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, fresh or dry. Straddled stance, arched back, repeated falling, forelegs first. Constipation, bloat, drooling, vomiting. Death (respiratory and heart failure). Most often no tissue changes.; Comments and Treatment: Young plants and seeds more toxic. Toxicity decreases with maturity.
Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Summer and Fall

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Black locust, False acacia, Locust tree; Robinia pseudoacacia; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods, roadsides, pinelands, on clay soils preferably; eastern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, although flowers have been suggested as the toxic principles. Diarrhea, loss of appetite, weakness, hind end paralysis, depression, dilated pupils, cold extremities; frequently weak pulse. Death infrequent; recovery period extensive. Tissue changes after death restricted to stomach and intestinal tract.; Comments and Treatment: Laxatives and stimulants suggested. Treatment supportive.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Dogbanes; Apocynum species; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods, roadsides, fields; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves and stems of green or dry plants. Increased temperature and pulse, dilated pupils, loss of appetite, discolored mucous membranes, cold extremities, death.; Comments and Treatment: Intravenous fluids and stomach protectants suggested.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Flatweed, Cat’s-ear, Gosmore; Hypochaeris radicata; Habitat and Distribution: Native to the Mediterranean and South America; widely distributed in the US, including Pacific, eastern and southeastern states; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Unknown; associated with but not proven cause of a neurologic condition called stringhalt, sudden onset of abnormal gait, knuckling of lower limb joints; paralysis of larynx; recovery possible, but condition could be permanent.; Comments and Treatment: Tranquilizers, sedatives, mephenesin, and thiamine (questionable effectiveness); longterm phenytoin therapy seems helpful. Treatment with baclofen also reported helpful. Surgery reported helpful for gait problems.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Nightshades, Jerusalem cherry, Potato, Horse nettle, Buffalo bur; Solanum species; Habitat and Distribution: Fence rows, waste areas, grain and hay fields; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves, shoots, and unripe berries. Inflammation of the stomach and intestine with bleeding, weakness, excess drooling, difficulty breathing, trembling, progressive paralysis, laying down, death.; Comments and Treatment: Pilocarpine, physostigmine, gastrointestinal protectants. Seeds may contaminate grain.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Perilla mint, Beefsteak plant; Perilla frutescens; Habitat and Distribution: Ornamental originally from India, escaped to moist pastures, fields, roadsides, and waste places; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Green or dry plant. Signs 2 to 10 days after exposure include difficulty breathing (especially on exhaling), open-mouth breathing, lowered head, reluctance to move, death on exertion. Tissue changes include fluid and swelling in the lungs.; Comments and Treatment: Treatment ineffective once signs are severe. Injectable steroids, antihistamines, and antibiotics may help. Handle gently (prevents exertion and death).

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Red maple; Acer rubrum; Habitat and Distribution: Moist land and swamps; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Wilted leaves. Anemia, and destruction of blood cells; weakness, rapid breathing, rapid heart beat, depression, jaundice, poor oxygenation of blood, brownish discoloration of blood and urine.; Comments and Treatment: Not common. Fluids, oxygen, and blood transfusion can be helpful. Methylene blue therapy not rewarding.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Russian knapweed; Centaurea repens; Habitat and Distribution: Waste areas, roadsides, railroads, and overgrazed rangeland; not common in cultivated or irrigated pastures; mostly western and upper midwestern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Fresh or dried plant. Chronic exposure, but sudden onset of signs. Inability to eat or drink, loss of facial tone, chewing, yawning, standing with head down, severe facial swelling, gait normal, head pressing, aimless walking or excitement most severe the first 2 days, become static thereafter. Death from starvation, dehydration, aspiration pneumonia.; Comments and Treatment: More toxic than yellow star thistle ( C. solstitialis ; see below) but with similar pathology and prognosis. Some relief with massive doses of atropine but not an effective treatment. Euthanasia recommended.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: White snakeroot; Eupatorium rugosum; Habitat and Distribution: Woods, cleared areas, waste places, usually the moister and richer soils; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Sheep, cattle, horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Complex benzyl alcohol (tremetol in leaves and stems). Excreted via milk; cumulative. Weight loss, weakness, trembling (muzzle and legs) prominent after exercise, constipation, acetone odor, fatty degeneration of liver, partial paralysis of throat, death in 1 to 3 days.; Comments and Treatment: “Milk sickness” or “trembles.” Supportive treatment. Heart and respiratory stimulants and laxatives may be necessary. Remove animal from access to plant.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Yellow star thistle, Yellow knapweed; Centaurea solstitialis; Habitat and Distribution: Waste areas, roadsides, pastures; mostly western North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant. Involuntary chewing movements, twitching of lips, flicking of tongue. Mouth commonly held open. Unable to eat; death from dehydration, starvation, aspiration pneumonia.; Comments and Treatment: Horses graze because of lack of other forage. Extended period of consumption essential for toxicity. Death of certain brain areas is diagnostic. No treatment. Euthanasia recommended.
Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Fall and Winter

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Black walnut; Juglans nigra; Habitat and Distribution: Native to eastern US; now from eastern seacoast, west to Michigan and most of the Midwest, south to Georgia and Texas; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Shavings with as little as 20% black walnut are toxic within 24 hours of exposure. Reluctance to move; depression; increased temperature, pulse, respiration rate, abdominal sounds, digital pulse, hoof temperature; distal limb swelling; lameness. Severe laminitis with continued exposure.; Comments and Treatment: Nonfatal; laminitis and edema of lower limbs. Remove shavings promptly. Treat for limb edema and laminitis. Improvement in 1 to 2 days with no complications.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Bladderpod, Rattlebox, Sesbane, Coffeebean; Sesbania vesicaria; Habitat and Distribution: Mostly open, low ground, abandoned cultivated fields; southeastern US coastal plain; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Green plant and seeds.; Comments and Treatment: Green seeds are more toxic. Remove animal from source immediately. General supportive treatment—saline purgatives, intravenous fluids.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Onions, (cultivated and wild); Allium cepa, A. canadense; Habitat and Distribution: Cultivated and grown on rich soils throughout US; Affected Animal(s): Cattle, horses, dogs; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire parts. Livestock readily consume onions; low blood cell counts develop within days of exposure. Signs are hemoglobin in the urine, diarrhea, loss of appetite, jaundice, incoordination, collapse, and possible death if untreated. Hemolytic anemia reported in livestock ingesting wild onions. Swollen, pale, dying liver.; Comments and Treatment: Signs similar to toxicity induced by S-methylcysteine sulfoxide (a rare toxic amino acid in Brassica species) in livestock. Susceptibility to onion poisoning varies across animal species: cattle more susceptible than horses and dogs, which are more susceptible than sheep and goats. Remove animals from source and prevent future access to cull onions. Symptomatic and supportive care essential.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Rattlebox, Purple serbane; Daubentonia unica; Habitat and Distribution: Cultivated and escaped, in waste places; southeastern US coastal plain; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Rapid pulse, weak respiration, diarrhea, death.; Comments and Treatment: Seeds poisonous. Remove animal from source. Saline purgatives.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Rayless goldenrod, Burroweed; Haplopappus heterophyllus; Habitat and Distribution: Dry plains, grasslands, open woodlands, and along irrigation canals; southwest US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Primarily nursing young and nonlactating animals. Reluctance to move, trembling, weakness, vomiting, difficulty breathing, constipation, lying down, coma, death.; Comments and Treatment: “Milk sickness.” Separate foals from mares.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Sweet clover, White sweet clover; Melilotus officinalis and M. alba; Habitat and Distribution: Commonly found on alkaline soils, fields, roadsides, and waste places; forage crop in southern and northern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: See also .; Comments and Treatment: See also .
Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Fall, Winter, and Spring

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Chinaberry; Melia azedarach; Habitat and Distribution: Fence rows, brush, waste places; southeastern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, fruit most toxic. Restlessness, vomiting, constipation, blue-tinged gums, rapid pulse, difficulty breathing, death within 24 hours.; Comments and Treatment: Gastroenteritis usual. Recovery may be spontaneous. Laxatives and stomach and intestinal protectants suggested.
Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: All Seasons

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Astragalus species (certain species only—selenium accumulators); Habitat and Distribution: Areas high in selenium, mostly western and midwestern; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Selenium (chronic). Slow growth, reproductive failure, loss of hair, sore feet, acute death.; Comments and Treatment: Avoid grazing seleniferous plants for extended periods. See also .

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Bracken fern; Pteridium aquilinum; Habitat and Distribution: Dry poor soil, open woods, sandy ridges; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: See also .; Comments and Treatment: See also .

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Castor bean; Ricinus communis; Habitat and Distribution: Cultivated in southern regions; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, seeds especially toxic. Short to long course (death or recovery). Violent purgation, straining with bloody diarrhea, weakness, drooling, trembling, incoordination.; Comments and Treatment: Diagnosis based on presence of seeds, red blood cell clumping, precipitin test. Specific antiserum, ideal antidote; sedatives, arecoline hydrobromide, followed by saline cathartics suggested.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Chokecherries, Wild cherries, Peaches; Prunus species; Habitat and Distribution: Waste areas, fence rows, woods, orchards, prairies, dry slopes; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Excitement leading to depression, difficulty breathing, incoordination, convulsions, prostration. Death may occur in 15 minutes.; Comments and Treatment: Mucous membranes, bright pink color; blood, bright red color (see also ).

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Corn cockle; Agrostemma githago; Habitat and Distribution: Weed, grainfields, and waste areas; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Seeds. Short course. Profuse watery diarrhea, vomiting, dullness, general weakness, rapid breathing, hemoglobin in the urine, death.; Comments and Treatment: Oils and stomach and intestinal protectants. Neutralize toxin. Blood transfusions may be necessary.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Crotalaria, Rattlebox; Crotalaria species; Habitat and Distribution: Fields and roadsides; eastern and central US; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, especially seeds. Chronic course. Horses—unthriftiness, incoordination, walking in circles, jaundice; Death may occur from a few weeks to months after ingestion.; Comments and Treatment: Cumulative, fresh or dry. No treatment.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Day-blooming jessamine and night-blooming jessamine, respectively; Cestrum diurnum, C. nocturnum; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods and fields; Gulf Coast states (Florida, Texas) and California; Affected Animal(s): Horses, and dogs (ingesting cholecalciferol-based rodenticides); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, including fruit and sap. Inflammation of the stomach and intestine develops on ingestion of fruits. Vomiting, depression, loss of appetite, chronic weight loss with normal appetite, choppy stiff gait, increased pulse, persistent increases in blood calcemia and phosphate, calcium deposits in arteries, tendons, ligaments, and kidneys, destruction of the parathyroid glands, overgrowth of the thyroid gland, and increased bone density reported with chronic ingestion of leaves.; Comments and Treatment: Prevent further access of animals to plants. In early stages, treatment might be effective. Correct fluid and electrolyte (salt) imbalances in cases with persistent vomiting or diarrhea. Reduce or prevent changes in blood calcium. Maintenance therapy of diuretics and steroids may be necessary.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Fraser’s photinia, Chinese photinia, Red leaf photinia, Red tip photinia; Photinia fraseri, P. serrulata, P. glabra; Habitat and Distribution: Common ornamental (hedge or screen) in southern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Same as for Nandina (see below).; Comments and Treatment: Same as for Nandina (see below).

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Groundsel, Senecio; Senecio species; Habitat and Distribution: Grassland areas; mostly western US; Affected Animal(s): Horses, limited to US; Toxic Parts and Effects: Fresh or dry. Short-term poisoning not common. Dullness, aimless walking, increased pulse, rapid breathing, weakness, colic, delayed death (days to months). Nervous signs evident in later stages.; Comments and Treatment: Liver biopsy diagnostic in early stages. No general treatment.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Hound’s tongue; Cynoglossum officinale; Habitat and Distribution: Common in waste places, roadsides, and pastured areas throughout US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Foliage. Unpleasant odor discourages consumption when fresh, becomes palatable in hay and is readily consumed. Signs are poor appetite, depression, rough hair coat, bleeding, bloody feces, incoordination, jaundice, death.; Comments and Treatment: Know source and quality of hay. Treatment symptomatic and supportive at best. Affected animals seldom recover.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Jimson weed, Thorn apple; Datura stramonium; Habitat and Distribution: Fields, barn lots, trampled pastures, and waste places on rich bottom soils; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, seeds in particular. Short course. Weak rapid pulse and heartbeat, dilated pupils, dry mouth, incoordination, convulsions, coma.; Comments and Treatment: All parts, mainly in hay or silage. Urine from animal dilates pupils of laboratory animals (diagnostic). Treatment nonspecific; cardiac and respiratory stimulants.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Johnson grass; Sorghum halepense; Habitat and Distribution: Weed of open fields and waste places; southern and scattered north to New York and Iowa; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Same as for Sorghum vulgare (see below).; Comments and Treatment: Same as for Sorghum vulgare (see below).

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Laurel, Ivybush, Lambkill; Kalmia species; Habitat and Distribution: Rich moist woods, meadows, or acid bogs; eastern and northwestern North America. Dangerous all seasons, especially winter and spring.; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Vegetative parts. Short course. Incoordination, excess drooling, vomiting, bloat, weakness, muscular spasms, coma, death.; Comments and Treatment: Treatment includes laxatives, demulcents, nerve stimulants, atropine.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Laurel cherry, Cherry laurel; Prunus caroliniana; Habitat and Distribution: Woods, fence rows, and often escaped from cultivation; southern regions. Dangerous all seasons, especially winter and spring.; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Wilted leaves, bark, and twigs. Short course. Difficult breathing, bloat, staggering, convulsions, followed by prostration and death. Mucous membranes and blood bright red.; Comments and Treatment: See also .

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Locoweed; Astragalus species, Oxytropis species (certain species only); Habitat and Distribution: Mostly western North America; Affected Animal(s): All grazing animals; Toxic Parts and Effects: Depression, emaciation, incoordination, dry lusterless hair. Abortions.; Comments and Treatment: Avoid grazing of source. Both green and dry plants toxic.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Lupines, Bluebonnet; Lupinus species; Habitat and Distribution: Dry to moist soils, roadsides, fields, and mountains; throughout, but poisoning mostly western North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Seeds (fresh and dry). Short course. No appetite, difficulty breathing, struggle, convulsions, death from respiratory paralysis.; Comments and Treatment: Do not disturb sick animals; remove from source as they begin to recover. No effective treatment, but survivors recover completely. See also .

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Milk vetch (and many other common names); Astragalus species (certain species only); Habitat and Distribution: Nearly all; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Hindlimb paralysis, goose-stepping, depression, rough coat, pulmonary emphysema, sudden death, spinal cord changes.; Comments and Treatment: Avoid grazing of pre-flower stage.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Milkweeds; Asclepias species; Habitat and Distribution: Dry areas, usually waste places, roadsides, streambeds; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, green or dry. Staggering, tetanic convulsions, bloating, difficulty breathing, dilated pupils, rapid and weak pulse, coma, death.; Comments and Treatment: Sedatives, laxatives, and intravenous fluids suggested.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Mustards, Crucifers, Cress; Brassica, Raphanus, Descurainia species; Habitat and Distribution: Fields, roadsides; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Seeds and vegetative parts, fresh or dry. Sudden or long course. Loss of appetite, severe inflammation of the stomach and intestines, drooling, diarrhea, paralysis, sensitivity to light, hemoglobin in the urine.; Comments and Treatment: Remove from source. Administer stomach and intestinal protectants (mineral oil).

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Nandina, Heavenly bamboo, Chinese sacred bamboo; Nandina domestica; Habitat and Distribution: Common ornamental in southern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Foliage and fruits. Hydrolyzed in stomach and intestinal tract to free cyanide, thereby affecting cellular respiration. Prognosis good if animal survives for 1 hour after signs begin. See also .; Comments and Treatment: Acute outcome precludes effective treatment for most; Intravenous sodium nitrite/sodium thiosulfate treatment of choice. Picrate test indicates toxic potential of the plant. See also .

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Oleander; Nerium oleander; Habitat and Distribution: Common ornamental in southern regions of the US; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, fresh or dry. Short course. Severe inflammation of the intestine and stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, increased pulse rate, weakness, death.; Comments and Treatment: No specific treatment. Atropine in conjunction with propranolol reported helpful.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Poison hemlock; Conium maculatum; Habitat and Distribution: Roadside ditches, damp waste areas; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Vegetative parts. Short course. Dilated pupils; weakness; staggering gait; slow pulse, progressing to rapid and thready. Slow, irregular breathing; death from respiratory failure.; Comments and Treatment: Toxin excreted via lungs and kidneys, mousy odor of breath and urine diagnostic. Administer saline cathartics; neutralize alkaloids with tannic acid, together with stimulants.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Privet, Ligustrum, Hedge plant; Ligustrum species; Habitat and Distribution: An ornamental; common as hedge; found at abandoned farm home sites, along fences, and in bottomlands.; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves and fruit. Primarily intestine and stomach irritants. Diarrhea, abdominal pain, incoordination, muscle weakness, weak pulse, fever, convulsions, sometimes death.; Comments and Treatment: Treatment symptomatic and supportive; correct dehydration.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Sorghum, Sudan grass, Kafir, Durra, Milo, Broom-corn, Schrock; Sorghum vulgare; Habitat and Distribution: Forage crops and escapes; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Heavy in vegetative parts. Short course. Difficult breathing, bloat, staggering, convulsions, death. Blood bright red (cyanide) or chocolate brown (nitrate).; Comments and Treatment: Hay safe for cyanide (volatile), not safe for nitrate (analyze). See also and .

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: St. John’s-wort, Goatweed, Klamath weed; Hypericum perforatum; Habitat and Distribution: Dry soil, roadsides, pastures, ranges; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Photodynamic pigment (hypericin). Short course. Sensitivity to light, pruritus and erythema, blindness, convulsions, diarrhea, hypersensitivity to cold water contact, death.; Comments and Treatment: Remove animals from source and sunlight. Corticosteroids given by injection, topical antibiotics.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Tall fescue; Festuca arundinacea; Habitat and Distribution: A coarse, hardy, drought-resistant grass; Pacific Northwest, Missouri, Oklahoma, and Kentucky; major pasture grass in southeastern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: See also .; Comments and Treatment: See also .

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Yellow jessamine, Evening trumpet flower, Carolina Jessamine; Gelsemium sempervirens; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods, thickets; southeast; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant. Short course. Weakness, incoordination, dilated pupils, convulsions, coma, death within 48 hours.; Comments and Treatment: No specific treatment. Relaxants and sedatives suggested.

Vital sign reference — Common and Scientific Names: Yew; Taxus species; Habitat and Distribution: Most of North America; Japanese and English yew common ornamentals; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Bark, leaves, seeds. Gaseous distress, diarrhea, vomiting, tremors, difficulty breathing, dilated pupils, respiratory difficulty, weakness, fatigue, collapse, coma, convulsions, irregular heartbeat, circulatory failure, death. Death may be rapid.; Comments and Treatment: Poisoning usually results when branches and trimmings fed to livestock.

Vital sign reference — Entire plant is toxic. Milk of lactating animals is a major excretory pathway. Observed signs are thirst, difficult swallowing, abdominal pain, profuse vomiting and diarrhea, weakness, and shock within hours of ingestion. Death from respiratory failure.

Vital sign reference — Prolonged course due to slow excretion of the toxin. Flush out stomach contents; supportive care for dehydration and electrolyte losses (fluid therapy); central nervous system, circulatory, and respiratory disturbances. Analgesics and atropine recommended for abdominal pain and diarrhea.

Vital sign reference — All above-ground parts (leaves in particular) reported toxic to cattle, horses, goats, rabbits, canaries, ostriches, and fish. Toxicity associated with loss of milk production (cattle, rabbits, goats), lung congestion, irregular heart beat, swelling of the jaw, sudden death (rabbits, caged birds, goats), respiratory distress, generalized congestion, subcutaneous swelling, and fluid around the heart (suggestive of cardiac failure, caged birds). In caged birds, signs may be seen within 24 hours (usually after 12 or more hours), with death 1 to 2 days after exposure.

Vital sign reference — Entire plant is toxic. Ingestion causes immediate intense pain, irritation to mucous membranes, excess drooling, swollen tongue and pharynx, diarrhea, and difficulty breathing. Pets’ access to plant associated with rhizomes brought indoors for winter storage.
Vital sign reference — Entire plant is toxic. Generally, sudden abdominal pain, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, frequent urination, irregular slow pulse, tremors, convulsions, and rarely death.

Vital sign reference — Leaves, flowers, rhizome, and water in which flowers have been kept. Variable period before signs arise depending on dose. Stomach and intestinal signs (vomiting, trembling, abdominal pain, diarrhea), progressive heart irregularities, and death. High blood pressure in sudden cases. Inflammation of the stomach and intestine, bleeding of small capillaries throughout.

Vital sign reference — Remove animal from source. Effectiveness of emetics limited by antiemetic effect of THC (the toxic compound in the plant). Oral tannic acid, activated charcoal followed by saline cathartics have been recommended. Stimulants (cardiac and respiratory) along with supportive therapy essential in severely depressed animals. Recovery slow at best (see also ).

Vital sign reference — Entire plant is toxic. On ingestion, immediate pain, local irritation to mucous membranes, excessive drooling, swollen tongue and pharynx, difficulty breathing, and kidney system failure. Excitability, nervous spasms, convulsions, and occasional brain swelling reported in cats.
Vital sign reference — Milky sap. Irritates mucous membranes and causes excessive drooling and vomiting but not death.
Vital sign reference — Leaves. Mucous membrane irritation, drooling, loss of appetite, vomiting, and if severe enough, diarrhea.
Vital sign reference — In severely depressed animals, stimulants (respiratory and cardiac), along with supportive therapy recommended.

Vital sign reference — Seeds, leaves, stems; seeds more toxic. Loss of appetite, hindleg weakness, knuckling of fetlock, listlessness, excess drooling, subnormal temperature, frequent urination. Tissue changes include inflammation of the stomach and intestine, with bleeding on heart and under liver capsule.

Vital sign reference — Seeds and young seedlings. Loss of appetite, depression, nausea, vomiting, weakness, rapid weak pulse, difficulty breathing, muscle spasms, convulsions. Tissue changes include inflammation of the stomach, intestines, liver, and kidney.
Vital sign reference — Entire plant. Drooling, vomiting, muscle weakness, incoordination or laying down, fast weak pulse, coma, death. No distinctive tissue changes.

Vital sign reference — Young leaves and swollen or sprouting acorns. Loss of appetite, constipation, followed by dark tarry diarrhea, dry muzzle, frequent urination, rapid weak pulse, death. Tissue changes include swelling around the kidneys with inflammation, inflammation of the stomach and intestine.

Vital sign reference — Entire plant; roots most toxic. Vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, low blood cell counts. Terminal convulsions, death from respiratory failure. Tissue changes include open inflammation of the stomach and intestine, bleeding of the mucosa, dark liver.
Vital sign reference — Entire plant, especially seeds and leaves. Depression, incoordination, twitching, paralysis, inflammation of mucous membranes.

Vital sign reference — Entire plant. Associated with stomach and intestinal dysfunction and degeneration of muscle. No fever, incoordination with diarrhea and coffee-colored urine. Affected animals are unable to stand but eat and are alert shortly before death. High blood pressure frequent. Tissue changes include heart and skeletal muscle degeneration. Congestion, fatty degeneration and tissue death in the liver and kidneys also reported. Death probably due to high blood pressure causing heart failure.
Vital sign reference — Entire plant. Drooling, vomiting, rapid and irregular respiration, weakness, death from respiratory failure.

Vital sign reference — Entire plant, fresh or dry. Straddled stance, arched back, repeated falling, forelegs first. Constipation, bloat, drooling, vomiting. Death (respiratory and heart failure). Most often no tissue changes.

Vital sign reference — Entire plant, although flowers have been suggested as the toxic principles. Diarrhea, loss of appetite, weakness, hind end paralysis, depression, dilated pupils, cold extremities; frequently weak pulse. Death infrequent; recovery period extensive. Tissue changes after death restricted to stomach and intestinal tract.
Vital sign reference — Leaves and stems of green or dry plants. Increased temperature and pulse, dilated pupils, loss of appetite, discolored mucous membranes, cold extremities, death.
Vital sign reference — “Milk sickness” or “trembles.” Supportive treatment. Heart and respiratory stimulants and laxatives may be necessary. Remove animal from access to plant.

Vital sign reference — Shavings with as little as 20% black walnut are toxic within 24 hours of exposure. Reluctance to move; depression; increased temperature, pulse, respiration rate, abdominal sounds, digital pulse, hoof temperature; distal limb swelling; lameness. Severe laminitis with continued exposure.
Vital sign reference — Rapid pulse, weak respiration, diarrhea, death.
Vital sign reference — Entire plant, fruit most toxic. Restlessness, vomiting, constipation, blue-tinged gums, rapid pulse, difficulty breathing, death within 24 hours.
Vital sign reference — Mucous membranes, bright pink color; blood, bright red color (see also ).

Vital sign reference — Entire plant, including fruit and sap. Inflammation of the stomach and intestine develops on ingestion of fruits. Vomiting, depression, loss of appetite, chronic weight loss with normal appetite, choppy stiff gait, increased pulse, persistent increases in blood calcemia and phosphate, calcium deposits in arteries, tendons, ligaments, and kidneys, destruction of the parathyroid glands, overgrowth of the thyroid gland, and increased bone density reported with chronic ingestion of leaves.

Vital sign reference — Fresh or dry. Short-term poisoning not common. Dullness, aimless walking, increased pulse, rapid breathing, weakness, colic, delayed death (days to months). Nervous signs evident in later stages.
Vital sign reference — Entire plant, seeds in particular. Short course. Weak rapid pulse and heartbeat, dilated pupils, dry mouth, incoordination, convulsions, coma.
Vital sign reference — All parts, mainly in hay or silage. Urine from animal dilates pupils of laboratory animals (diagnostic). Treatment nonspecific; cardiac and respiratory stimulants.
Vital sign reference — Wilted leaves, bark, and twigs. Short course. Difficult breathing, bloat, staggering, convulsions, followed by prostration and death. Mucous membranes and blood bright red.
Vital sign reference — Seeds (fresh and dry). Short course. No appetite, difficulty breathing, struggle, convulsions, death from respiratory paralysis.
Vital sign reference — Entire plant, green or dry. Staggering, tetanic convulsions, bloating, difficulty breathing, dilated pupils, rapid and weak pulse, coma, death.
Vital sign reference — Entire plant, fresh or dry. Short course. Severe inflammation of the intestine and stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, increased pulse rate, weakness, death.

Vital sign reference — Vegetative parts. Short course. Dilated pupils; weakness; staggering gait; slow pulse, progressing to rapid and thready. Slow, irregular breathing; death from respiratory failure.
Vital sign reference — Leaves and fruit. Primarily intestine and stomach irritants. Diarrhea, abdominal pain, incoordination, muscle weakness, weak pulse, fever, convulsions, sometimes death.

Vital sign reference — Bark, leaves, seeds. Gaseous distress, diarrhea, vomiting, tremors, difficulty breathing, dilated pupils, respiratory difficulty, weakness, fatigue, collapse, coma, convulsions, irregular heartbeat, circulatory failure, death. Death may be rapid.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Autumn crocus, Crocus, Fall crocus, Meadow saffron, Wonder bulb; Scientific Name (Family): Colchicum autumnale (Liliaceae, Colchicaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant is toxic. Milk of lactating animals is a major excretory pathway. Observed signs are thirst, difficult swallowing, abdominal pain, profuse vomiting and diarrhea, weakness, and shock within hours of ingestion. Death from respiratory failure.; Treatment: Prolonged course due to slow excretion of the toxin. Flush out stomach contents; supportive care for dehydration and electrolyte losses (fluid therapy); central nervous system, circulatory, and respiratory disturbances. Analgesics and atropine recommended for abdominal pain and diarrhea.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Avocado pear, Alligator pear; Scientific Name (Family): Persea americana (Lauraceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: All above-ground parts (leaves in particular) reported toxic to cattle, horses, goats, rabbits, canaries, ostriches, and fish. Toxicity associated with loss of milk production (cattle, rabbits, goats), lung congestion, irregular heart beat, swelling of the jaw, sudden death (rabbits, caged birds, goats), respiratory distress, generalized congestion, subcutaneous swelling, and fluid around the heart (suggestive of cardiac failure, caged birds). In caged birds, signs may be seen within 24 hours (usually after 12 or more hours), with death 1 to 2 days after exposure.; Treatment: Primarily symptomatic and supportive (see also )

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Azalea, Rhododendron; Scientific Name (Family): Rhododendron species (Ericaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, including pollen and nectar. Within hours of ingestion of toxic dose (1 gram/kilogram), drooling, tearing, vomiting, diarrhea, difficulty breathing, muscle weakness, convulsions, coma, and death. Signs may last several days, but toxin is not cumulative.; Treatment: Supportive; flush out stomach contents, activated charcoal, saline cathartics, calcium injection, and antibiotics to control possible pneumonia suggested.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Barbados aloe, Curacao aloe; Scientific Name (Family): Aloe Barbadensis (Liliaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Latex of the leaves; higher concentrations in younger leaves. Upon eating, causes abrupt, severe diarrhea and/or low blood sugar, with vomiting in some cases.; Treatment: Supportive; control diarrhea and fluid loss.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Caladium, Fancy leaf caladium, Angel wings; Scientific Name (Family): Caladium species (Araceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant is toxic. Ingestion causes immediate intense pain, irritation to mucous membranes, excess drooling, swollen tongue and pharynx, diarrhea, and difficulty breathing. Pets’ access to plant associated with rhizomes brought indoors for winter storage.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Century plant, American aloe; Scientific Name (Family): Agave americana (Agavaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves, seeds, and sap. Upon eating, causes skin and mouth irritation and swelling.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Cherry pepper, Chili pepper, Ornamental pepper, Capsicum; Scientific Name (Family): Capsicum annuum (Solanaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Capsaicinoids (capsaicin) in the mature fruits, solanine and scopoletin in foliage; irritating to the stomach and intestinal tract, with vomiting and diarrhea. Not likely to be lethal.; Treatment: Supportive; irritation relief—flush with cool water, topical or oral mineral or vegetable oil. Rarely topical anesthetics.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Chinese evergreen, Painted drop tongue; Scientific Name (Family): Aglaonema modestum (Araceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant. Upon eating, causes mouth irritation and swelling.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Coontie, Florida arrowroot, Seminole bread, Cycad; Scientific Name (Family): Zamia pumila (Zamiaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves, seeds, and stem. Ingestion associated with liver and stomach and intestinal disturbances and incoordination. Signs are persistent vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, depression, and muscular paralysis.; Treatment: No specific therapy; intravenous fluids and supportive care recommended.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Cyclamen, Snowbread, Shooting star; Scientific Name (Family): Cyclamen species (Primulaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Tuberous rhizomes cause stomach and intestine irritation, thereby increasing absorption and severe toxicity. Reduced appetite, diarrhea, convulsions, and paralysis can occur. Pets have greater access to these plants over winter months (both pets and plants are indoors).; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Daffodils; Scientific Name (Family): Narcissus species (Amaryllidaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Same as for hyacinths ( see below).; Treatment: Same as for hyacinths ( see below).

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Dragon tree; Scientific Name (Family): Dracaena species (Agavaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves. Vomiting and severe diarrhea indicative of stomach and intestinal irritation expected. No cases have been reported.; Treatment: Supportive, to correct fluid and electrolyte (salt) imbalance.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Dumbcane; Scientific Name (Family): Dieffenbachia species (Araceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, including sap. On ingestion, immediate intense pain, burning, and inflammation of mouth and throat, no appetite, vomiting, and possibly diarrhea, with tongue extended, head shaking, excessive drooling, and difficulty breathing. Immediate pain limits amount consumed. Death infrequent.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Easter lily, Trumpet lily; Scientific Name (Family): Lilium longiflorum; L. tigrinum (Liliaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant is toxic. Kidney system failure in cats 2 to 4 days post-ingestion. Not reported toxic to other species. Vomiting, depression, loss of appetite within 12 hours post-ingestion.; Treatment: Emetics (induce vomiting), activated charcoal, saline cathartic, and nursing care—as for renal failure—within hours of ingestion. Delayed treatment is associated with poor prognosis.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: English holly, European holly; Scientific Name (Family): Ilex aquifolium (Aquifoliaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves, fruits, and seeds. Abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea seen after ingestion of 2 or more berries. Death is rare.; Treatment: Supportive (at best)

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Foxglove; Scientific Name (Family): Digitalis purpurea (Scrophulariacae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant is toxic. Generally, sudden abdominal pain, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, frequent urination, irregular slow pulse, tremors, convulsions, and rarely death.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Hyacinths; Scientific Name (Family): Hyacinthus species (Liliaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Bulbs. After ingestion of toxic dose (bulbs), vomiting, diarrhea, and rare deaths reported. Bulbs in storage may be accessible to pets.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Jerusalem cherry; Scientific Name (Family): Solanum pseudocapsicum (Solanaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves and fruits. Loss of appetite, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea with blood, drooling, progressive weakness or paralysis, difficulty breathing, irregular heartbeat, circulatory collapse, dilated pupils, and convulsions reported.; Treatment: Supportive; flush out stomach contents, activated charcoal, electrolytes and fluids, and anticonvulsants suggested.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Kalanchoe, Air-plant, Cathedral-bells; Scientific Name (Family): Kalanchoe species (Crassulaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves. Within hours of ingesting toxic dose, depression, rapid breathing, teeth grinding, lack of coordination, paralysis, muscle spasms (rabbit), and death (rat).; Treatment: Supportive; atropine has been effective in rabbits.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Lily-of-the-valley, Conval lily, Mayflower; Scientific Name (Family): Convallaria majalis (Liliaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves, flowers, rhizome, and water in which flowers have been kept. Variable period before signs arise depending on dose. Stomach and intestinal signs (vomiting, trembling, abdominal pain, diarrhea), progressive heart irregularities, and death. High blood pressure in sudden cases. Inflammation of the stomach and intestine, bleeding of small capillaries throughout.; Treatment: Aimed at gut decontamination (flushing of stomach contents) and at correcting irregular heart beats and electrolyte (salt) imbalances. Monitoring of EKG and serum potassium necessary.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Marijuana, Mary Jane, Grass, Pot, Hashish, Indian hemp, Reefer, Weed; Scientific Name (Family): Cannabis sativa (Cannabaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves, stems, and flower buds of mature plants or edible products intended for people that contain tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Lethal dose for dogs is more than 3 grams/kilogram body weight. Pets’ exposure usually from accidental access to this plant being used for medical or recreational uses by owner. Pets (dogs primarily) show incoordination, vomiting, dilated pupils, prolonged depression, excessive or irregular heartbeats, drooling, hyperexcitability, tremors, and fever. Death results when vital central nervous system regulatory centers are severely depressed.; Treatment: Remove animal from source. Effectiveness of emetics limited by antiemetic effect of THC (the toxic compound in the plant). Oral tannic acid, activated charcoal followed by saline cathartics have been recommended. Stimulants (cardiac and respiratory) along with supportive therapy essential in severely depressed animals. Recovery slow at best (see also ).

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Mistletoe; Scientific Name (Family): Phoradendron flavescens (Viscaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant is toxic. Vomiting, profuse diarrhea, dilated pupils, rapid labored breathing, shock, and death from cardiovascular collapse within hours of ingesting toxic dose.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Philodendron; Scientific Name (Family): Philodendron species (Araceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant is toxic. On ingestion, immediate pain, local irritation to mucous membranes, excessive drooling, swollen tongue and pharynx, difficulty breathing, and kidney system failure. Excitability, nervous spasms, convulsions, and occasional brain swelling reported in cats.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Poinsettia, Christmas flower, Christmas star; Scientific Name (Family): Euphorbia pulcherrima (Euphorbiaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Milky sap. Irritates mucous membranes and causes excessive drooling and vomiting but not death.; Treatment: Supportive; flush out stomach contents, activated charcoal, and saline cathartics should be considered.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Sansevieria, Snake plant, Mother-in-law’s tongue; Scientific Name (Family): Sansevieria species (Agavaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves and flowers. Vomiting, drooling, diarrhea, and rupture of red blood cells related to stomach and intestinal activity of these compounds.; Treatment: Supportive; fluids and electrolytes may be necessary.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Schefflera, Umbrella tree; Scientific Name (Family): Schefflera species (Araliaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves. Mucous membrane irritation, drooling, loss of appetite, vomiting, and if severe enough, diarrhea.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Spider plant, St. Bernard’s lily, Airplane plant; Scientific Name (Family): Chlorophytum species (Liliaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves and plantlets. Vomiting, drooling, retching, and varying degrees of loss of appetite seen in cats within hours of ingestion. Deaths and diarrhea not reported.; Treatment: Supportive

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Yesterday-today-and-tomorrow, Lady-of-the-night; Scientific Name (Family): Brunfelsia pauciflora floribunda (Solanaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Flowers, leaves, bark, and roots. Upon eating, animals show abnormal heart rhythms, dry mouth, dilated pupils, difficulty breathing, tremors, depression, urinary retention, and sometimes coma (deep sedation). Not reported to cause death.; Treatment: In severely depressed animals, stimulants (respiratory and cardiac), along with supportive therapy recommended.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common Name: Yew; Scientific Name (Family): Taxus species (Taxaceae); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant except the fleshy aril (red covering of the seeds). Nervousness, trembling, incoordination, difficulty breathing, collapse; slowing of heartbeats progressing to the heart stopping and death without struggle. Empty right side of heart; dark, tarry blood in left side of heart.; Treatment: Supportive at best; usually futile once signs appear. Atropine may be helpful.
Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Spring and Fall

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Water hemlock; Cicuta species; Habitat and Distribution: Open, moist to wet environments; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Roots, stem base, young leaves. Toxicity retained when dry, except in hay. Rapid onset of signs, with death in 15 to 30 minutes. Drooling, muscular twitching, dilated pupils. Violent convulsions, coma, death. Poisoning in humans common.; Comments and Treatment: Sedatives to control spasm and heart action. Outlook good if alive 2 hours after ingestion.
Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Spring

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: African rue; Peganum harmala; Habitat and Distribution: Arid to semiarid ranges; southwest; Affected Animal(s): Horses likely; Toxic Parts and Effects: Seeds, leaves, stems; seeds more toxic. Loss of appetite, hindleg weakness, knuckling of fetlock, listlessness, excess drooling, subnormal temperature, frequent urination. Tissue changes include inflammation of the stomach and intestine, with bleeding on heart and under liver capsule.; Comments and Treatment: Unpalatable. Eaten only under drought conditions.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Cocklebur; Xanthium species; Habitat and Distribution: Fields, waste places, exposed shores of ponds or rivers; throughout North America. Dangerous season spring and occasionally fall.; Affected Animal(s): All animals; Toxic Parts and Effects: Seeds and young seedlings. Loss of appetite, depression, nausea, vomiting, weakness, rapid weak pulse, difficulty breathing, muscle spasms, convulsions. Tissue changes include inflammation of the stomach, intestines, liver, and kidney.; Comments and Treatment: Seedlings or grain contaminated with seeds. Oils and fats given by mouth may be beneficial; warmth, stimulants given in the muscle.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Death camas; Zygadenus species; Habitat and Distribution: Foothill grazing lands, occasionally boggy grasslands, low open woods; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant. Drooling, vomiting, muscle weakness, incoordination or laying down, fast weak pulse, coma, death. No distinctive tissue changes.; Comments and Treatment: Seeds most toxic. Leaves and stems lose toxicity as plant matures. Atropine and picrotoxin may be effective.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Oaks; Quercus species; Habitat and Distribution: Most deciduous woods; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Young leaves and swollen or sprouting acorns. Loss of appetite, constipation, followed by dark tarry diarrhea, dry muzzle, frequent urination, rapid weak pulse, death. Tissue changes include swelling around the kidneys with inflammation, inflammation of the stomach and intestine.; Comments and Treatment: Diet must consist of more than 50% oak buds and young leaves for a period of time. Kidney failure with diet history diagnostic. Treatment symptomatic. Oral ruminatorics helpful. (see also .)

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Pokeweed, Poke; Phytolacca americana; Habitat and Distribution: Disturbed rich soils such as recent clearings, pastures, waste areas; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses, people; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant; roots most toxic. Vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, low blood cell counts. Terminal convulsions, death from respiratory failure. Tissue changes include open inflammation of the stomach and intestine, bleeding of the mucosa, dark liver.; Comments and Treatment: Oils and protectants (stomach and intestinal tract). Dilute acetic acid orally, stimulants. Blood transfusion (hemolytic anemia).
Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Spring and Summer

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Buckeye; Aesculus species; Habitat and Distribution: Woods and thickets; eastern US and California; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, especially seeds and leaves. Depression, incoordination, twitching, paralysis, inflammation of mucous membranes.; Comments and Treatment: Young shoots and seeds especially poisonous. Stimulants and purgatives.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Coffeepod, Sicklepod; Cassia obtusifolia; Habitat and Distribution: Found in cultivated (corn, soybean, or sorghum) and abandoned fields, along fences, roadsides; naturalized in eastern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Toxic principles thought to be same as in Cassia occidentalis . Signs, although similar, less severe with Cassia obtusifolia .; Comments and Treatment: Treatment ineffective in down animals.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Coffee senna, Coffee weed, Styptic weed, Wild coffee; Cassia occidentalis; Habitat and Distribution: Common along roadsides, waste areas and pastures; naturalized in eastern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses, rabbits; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant. Associated with stomach and intestinal dysfunction and degeneration of muscle. No fever, incoordination with diarrhea and coffee-colored urine. Affected animals are unable to stand but eat and are alert shortly before death. High blood pressure frequent. Tissue changes include heart and skeletal muscle degeneration. Congestion, fatty degeneration and tissue death in the liver and kidneys also reported. Death probably due to high blood pressure causing heart failure.; Comments and Treatment: No specific treatment known. Symptomatic and supportive care essential. Although tissue changes are similar to those of vitamin E/selenium deficiency, this therapy is contraindicated. Remove animals from source.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Fly poison, Staggergrass, Crow poison; Amianthium muscaetoxicum; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods, fields, and acid bogs; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant. Drooling, vomiting, rapid and irregular respiration, weakness, death from respiratory failure.; Comments and Treatment: No practical treatment. Especially dangerous for animals new to pasture. Keep animals well fed.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Larkspurs; Delphinium species; Habitat and Distribution: Either cultivated or wild, usually in open foothills or meadows and among aspen; mostly western. Dangerous season spring and summer, also seeds in fall.; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, fresh or dry. Straddled stance, arched back, repeated falling, forelegs first. Constipation, bloat, drooling, vomiting. Death (respiratory and heart failure). Most often no tissue changes.; Comments and Treatment: Young plants and seeds more toxic. Toxicity decreases with maturity.
Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Summer and Fall

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Black locust, False acacia, Locust tree; Robinia pseudoacacia; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods, roadsides, pinelands, on clay soils preferably; eastern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, although flowers have been suggested as the toxic principles. Diarrhea, loss of appetite, weakness, hind end paralysis, depression, dilated pupils, cold extremities; frequently weak pulse. Death infrequent; recovery period extensive. Tissue changes after death restricted to stomach and intestinal tract.; Comments and Treatment: Laxatives and stimulants suggested. Treatment supportive.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Dogbanes; Apocynum species; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods, roadsides, fields; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves and stems of green or dry plants. Increased temperature and pulse, dilated pupils, loss of appetite, discolored mucous membranes, cold extremities, death.; Comments and Treatment: Intravenous fluids and stomach protectants suggested.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Flatweed, Cat’s-ear, Gosmore; Hypochaeris radicata; Habitat and Distribution: Native to the Mediterranean and South America; widely distributed in the US, including Pacific, eastern and southeastern states; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Unknown; associated with but not proven cause of a neurologic condition called stringhalt, sudden onset of abnormal gait, knuckling of lower limb joints; paralysis of larynx; recovery possible, but condition could be permanent.; Comments and Treatment: Tranquilizers, sedatives, mephenesin, and thiamine (questionable effectiveness); longterm phenytoin therapy seems helpful. Treatment with baclofen also reported helpful. Surgery reported helpful for gait problems.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Nightshades, Jerusalem cherry, Potato, Horse nettle, Buffalo bur; Solanum species; Habitat and Distribution: Fence rows, waste areas, grain and hay fields; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves, shoots, and unripe berries. Inflammation of the stomach and intestine with bleeding, weakness, excess drooling, difficulty breathing, trembling, progressive paralysis, laying down, death.; Comments and Treatment: Pilocarpine, physostigmine, gastrointestinal protectants. Seeds may contaminate grain.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Perilla mint, Beefsteak plant; Perilla frutescens; Habitat and Distribution: Ornamental originally from India, escaped to moist pastures, fields, roadsides, and waste places; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Green or dry plant. Signs 2 to 10 days after exposure include difficulty breathing (especially on exhaling), open-mouth breathing, lowered head, reluctance to move, death on exertion. Tissue changes include fluid and swelling in the lungs.; Comments and Treatment: Treatment ineffective once signs are severe. Injectable steroids, antihistamines, and antibiotics may help. Handle gently (prevents exertion and death).

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Red maple; Acer rubrum; Habitat and Distribution: Moist land and swamps; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Wilted leaves. Anemia, and destruction of blood cells; weakness, rapid breathing, rapid heart beat, depression, jaundice, poor oxygenation of blood, brownish discoloration of blood and urine.; Comments and Treatment: Not common. Fluids, oxygen, and blood transfusion can be helpful. Methylene blue therapy not rewarding.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Russian knapweed; Centaurea repens; Habitat and Distribution: Waste areas, roadsides, railroads, and overgrazed rangeland; not common in cultivated or irrigated pastures; mostly western and upper midwestern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Fresh or dried plant. Chronic exposure, but sudden onset of signs. Inability to eat or drink, loss of facial tone, chewing, yawning, standing with head down, severe facial swelling, gait normal, head pressing, aimless walking or excitement most severe the first 2 days, become static thereafter. Death from starvation, dehydration, aspiration pneumonia.; Comments and Treatment: More toxic than yellow star thistle ( C. solstitialis ; see below) but with similar pathology and prognosis. Some relief with massive doses of atropine but not an effective treatment. Euthanasia recommended.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: White snakeroot; Eupatorium rugosum; Habitat and Distribution: Woods, cleared areas, waste places, usually the moister and richer soils; eastern North America; Affected Animal(s): Sheep, cattle, horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Complex benzyl alcohol (tremetol in leaves and stems). Excreted via milk; cumulative. Weight loss, weakness, trembling (muzzle and legs) prominent after exercise, constipation, acetone odor, fatty degeneration of liver, partial paralysis of throat, death in 1 to 3 days.; Comments and Treatment: “Milk sickness” or “trembles.” Supportive treatment. Heart and respiratory stimulants and laxatives may be necessary. Remove animal from access to plant.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Yellow star thistle, Yellow knapweed; Centaurea solstitialis; Habitat and Distribution: Waste areas, roadsides, pastures; mostly western North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant. Involuntary chewing movements, twitching of lips, flicking of tongue. Mouth commonly held open. Unable to eat; death from dehydration, starvation, aspiration pneumonia.; Comments and Treatment: Horses graze because of lack of other forage. Extended period of consumption essential for toxicity. Death of certain brain areas is diagnostic. No treatment. Euthanasia recommended.
Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Fall and Winter

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Black walnut; Juglans nigra; Habitat and Distribution: Native to eastern US; now from eastern seacoast, west to Michigan and most of the Midwest, south to Georgia and Texas; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Shavings with as little as 20% black walnut are toxic within 24 hours of exposure. Reluctance to move; depression; increased temperature, pulse, respiration rate, abdominal sounds, digital pulse, hoof temperature; distal limb swelling; lameness. Severe laminitis with continued exposure.; Comments and Treatment: Nonfatal; laminitis and edema of lower limbs. Remove shavings promptly. Treat for limb edema and laminitis. Improvement in 1 to 2 days with no complications.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Bladderpod, Rattlebox, Sesbane, Coffeebean; Sesbania vesicaria; Habitat and Distribution: Mostly open, low ground, abandoned cultivated fields; southeastern US coastal plain; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Green plant and seeds.; Comments and Treatment: Green seeds are more toxic. Remove animal from source immediately. General supportive treatment—saline purgatives, intravenous fluids.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Onions, (cultivated and wild); Allium cepa, A. canadense; Habitat and Distribution: Cultivated and grown on rich soils throughout US; Affected Animal(s): Cattle, horses, dogs; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire parts. Livestock readily consume onions; low blood cell counts develop within days of exposure. Signs are hemoglobin in the urine, diarrhea, loss of appetite, jaundice, incoordination, collapse, and possible death if untreated. Hemolytic anemia reported in livestock ingesting wild onions. Swollen, pale, dying liver.; Comments and Treatment: Signs similar to toxicity induced by S-methylcysteine sulfoxide (a rare toxic amino acid in Brassica species) in livestock. Susceptibility to onion poisoning varies across animal species: cattle more susceptible than horses and dogs, which are more susceptible than sheep and goats. Remove animals from source and prevent future access to cull onions. Symptomatic and supportive care essential.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Rattlebox, Purple serbane; Daubentonia unica; Habitat and Distribution: Cultivated and escaped, in waste places; southeastern US coastal plain; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Rapid pulse, weak respiration, diarrhea, death.; Comments and Treatment: Seeds poisonous. Remove animal from source. Saline purgatives.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Rayless goldenrod, Burroweed; Haplopappus heterophyllus; Habitat and Distribution: Dry plains, grasslands, open woodlands, and along irrigation canals; southwest US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Primarily nursing young and nonlactating animals. Reluctance to move, trembling, weakness, vomiting, difficulty breathing, constipation, lying down, coma, death.; Comments and Treatment: “Milk sickness.” Separate foals from mares.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Sweet clover, White sweet clover; Melilotus officinalis and M. alba; Habitat and Distribution: Commonly found on alkaline soils, fields, roadsides, and waste places; forage crop in southern and northern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: See also .; Comments and Treatment: See also .
Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: Fall, Winter, and Spring

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Chinaberry; Melia azedarach; Habitat and Distribution: Fence rows, brush, waste places; southeastern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, fruit most toxic. Restlessness, vomiting, constipation, blue-tinged gums, rapid pulse, difficulty breathing, death within 24 hours.; Comments and Treatment: Gastroenteritis usual. Recovery may be spontaneous. Laxatives and stomach and intestinal protectants suggested.
Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Dangerous Season: All Seasons

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Astragalus species (certain species only—selenium accumulators); Habitat and Distribution: Areas high in selenium, mostly western and midwestern; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Selenium (chronic). Slow growth, reproductive failure, loss of hair, sore feet, acute death.; Comments and Treatment: Avoid grazing seleniferous plants for extended periods. See also .

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Bracken fern; Pteridium aquilinum; Habitat and Distribution: Dry poor soil, open woods, sandy ridges; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: See also .; Comments and Treatment: See also .

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Castor bean; Ricinus communis; Habitat and Distribution: Cultivated in southern regions; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, seeds especially toxic. Short to long course (death or recovery). Violent purgation, straining with bloody diarrhea, weakness, drooling, trembling, incoordination.; Comments and Treatment: Diagnosis based on presence of seeds, red blood cell clumping, precipitin test. Specific antiserum, ideal antidote; sedatives, arecoline hydrobromide, followed by saline cathartics suggested.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Chokecherries, Wild cherries, Peaches; Prunus species; Habitat and Distribution: Waste areas, fence rows, woods, orchards, prairies, dry slopes; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Excitement leading to depression, difficulty breathing, incoordination, convulsions, prostration. Death may occur in 15 minutes.; Comments and Treatment: Mucous membranes, bright pink color; blood, bright red color (see also ).

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Corn cockle; Agrostemma githago; Habitat and Distribution: Weed, grainfields, and waste areas; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Seeds. Short course. Profuse watery diarrhea, vomiting, dullness, general weakness, rapid breathing, hemoglobin in the urine, death.; Comments and Treatment: Oils and stomach and intestinal protectants. Neutralize toxin. Blood transfusions may be necessary.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Crotalaria, Rattlebox; Crotalaria species; Habitat and Distribution: Fields and roadsides; eastern and central US; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, especially seeds. Chronic course. Horses—unthriftiness, incoordination, walking in circles, jaundice; Death may occur from a few weeks to months after ingestion.; Comments and Treatment: Cumulative, fresh or dry. No treatment.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Day-blooming jessamine and night-blooming jessamine, respectively; Cestrum diurnum, C. nocturnum; Habitat and Distribution: Open woods and fields; Gulf Coast states (Florida, Texas) and California; Affected Animal(s): Horses, and dogs (ingesting cholecalciferol-based rodenticides); Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, including fruit and sap. Inflammation of the stomach and intestine develops on ingestion of fruits. Vomiting, depression, loss of appetite, chronic weight loss with normal appetite, choppy stiff gait, increased pulse, persistent increases in blood calcemia and phosphate, calcium deposits in arteries, tendons, ligaments, and kidneys, destruction of the parathyroid glands, overgrowth of the thyroid gland, and increased bone density reported with chronic ingestion of leaves.; Comments and Treatment: Prevent further access of animals to plants. In early stages, treatment might be effective. Correct fluid and electrolyte (salt) imbalances in cases with persistent vomiting or diarrhea. Reduce or prevent changes in blood calcium. Maintenance therapy of diuretics and steroids may be necessary.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Fraser’s photinia, Chinese photinia, Red leaf photinia, Red tip photinia; Photinia fraseri, P. serrulata, P. glabra; Habitat and Distribution: Common ornamental (hedge or screen) in southern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Same as for Nandina (see below).; Comments and Treatment: Same as for Nandina (see below).

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Groundsel, Senecio; Senecio species; Habitat and Distribution: Grassland areas; mostly western US; Affected Animal(s): Horses, limited to US; Toxic Parts and Effects: Fresh or dry. Short-term poisoning not common. Dullness, aimless walking, increased pulse, rapid breathing, weakness, colic, delayed death (days to months). Nervous signs evident in later stages.; Comments and Treatment: Liver biopsy diagnostic in early stages. No general treatment.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Hound’s tongue; Cynoglossum officinale; Habitat and Distribution: Common in waste places, roadsides, and pastured areas throughout US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Foliage. Unpleasant odor discourages consumption when fresh, becomes palatable in hay and is readily consumed. Signs are poor appetite, depression, rough hair coat, bleeding, bloody feces, incoordination, jaundice, death.; Comments and Treatment: Know source and quality of hay. Treatment symptomatic and supportive at best. Affected animals seldom recover.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Jimson weed, Thorn apple; Datura stramonium; Habitat and Distribution: Fields, barn lots, trampled pastures, and waste places on rich bottom soils; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, seeds in particular. Short course. Weak rapid pulse and heartbeat, dilated pupils, dry mouth, incoordination, convulsions, coma.; Comments and Treatment: All parts, mainly in hay or silage. Urine from animal dilates pupils of laboratory animals (diagnostic). Treatment nonspecific; cardiac and respiratory stimulants.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Johnson grass; Sorghum halepense; Habitat and Distribution: Weed of open fields and waste places; southern and scattered north to New York and Iowa; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Same as for Sorghum vulgare (see below).; Comments and Treatment: Same as for Sorghum vulgare (see below).

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Laurel, Ivybush, Lambkill; Kalmia species; Habitat and Distribution: Rich moist woods, meadows, or acid bogs; eastern and northwestern North America. Dangerous all seasons, especially winter and spring.; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Vegetative parts. Short course. Incoordination, excess drooling, vomiting, bloat, weakness, muscular spasms, coma, death.; Comments and Treatment: Treatment includes laxatives, demulcents, nerve stimulants, atropine.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Laurel cherry, Cherry laurel; Prunus caroliniana; Habitat and Distribution: Woods, fence rows, and often escaped from cultivation; southern regions. Dangerous all seasons, especially winter and spring.; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Wilted leaves, bark, and twigs. Short course. Difficult breathing, bloat, staggering, convulsions, followed by prostration and death. Mucous membranes and blood bright red.; Comments and Treatment: See also .

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Locoweed; Astragalus species, Oxytropis species (certain species only); Habitat and Distribution: Mostly western North America; Affected Animal(s): All grazing animals; Toxic Parts and Effects: Depression, emaciation, incoordination, dry lusterless hair. Abortions.; Comments and Treatment: Avoid grazing of source. Both green and dry plants toxic.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Lupines, Bluebonnet; Lupinus species; Habitat and Distribution: Dry to moist soils, roadsides, fields, and mountains; throughout, but poisoning mostly western North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Seeds (fresh and dry). Short course. No appetite, difficulty breathing, struggle, convulsions, death from respiratory paralysis.; Comments and Treatment: Do not disturb sick animals; remove from source as they begin to recover. No effective treatment, but survivors recover completely. See also .

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Milk vetch (and many other common names); Astragalus species (certain species only); Habitat and Distribution: Nearly all; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Hindlimb paralysis, goose-stepping, depression, rough coat, pulmonary emphysema, sudden death, spinal cord changes.; Comments and Treatment: Avoid grazing of pre-flower stage.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Milkweeds; Asclepias species; Habitat and Distribution: Dry areas, usually waste places, roadsides, streambeds; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, green or dry. Staggering, tetanic convulsions, bloating, difficulty breathing, dilated pupils, rapid and weak pulse, coma, death.; Comments and Treatment: Sedatives, laxatives, and intravenous fluids suggested.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Mustards, Crucifers, Cress; Brassica, Raphanus, Descurainia species; Habitat and Distribution: Fields, roadsides; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Seeds and vegetative parts, fresh or dry. Sudden or long course. Loss of appetite, severe inflammation of the stomach and intestines, drooling, diarrhea, paralysis, sensitivity to light, hemoglobin in the urine.; Comments and Treatment: Remove from source. Administer stomach and intestinal protectants (mineral oil).

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Nandina, Heavenly bamboo, Chinese sacred bamboo; Nandina domestica; Habitat and Distribution: Common ornamental in southern US; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Foliage and fruits. Hydrolyzed in stomach and intestinal tract to free cyanide, thereby affecting cellular respiration. Prognosis good if animal survives for 1 hour after signs begin. See also .; Comments and Treatment: Acute outcome precludes effective treatment for most; Intravenous sodium nitrite/sodium thiosulfate treatment of choice. Picrate test indicates toxic potential of the plant. See also .

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Oleander; Nerium oleander; Habitat and Distribution: Common ornamental in southern regions of the US; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Entire plant, fresh or dry. Short course. Severe inflammation of the intestine and stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, increased pulse rate, weakness, death.; Comments and Treatment: No specific treatment. Atropine in conjunction with propranolol reported helpful.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Poison hemlock; Conium maculatum; Habitat and Distribution: Roadside ditches, damp waste areas; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Vegetative parts. Short course. Dilated pupils; weakness; staggering gait; slow pulse, progressing to rapid and thready. Slow, irregular breathing; death from respiratory failure.; Comments and Treatment: Toxin excreted via lungs and kidneys, mousy odor of breath and urine diagnostic. Administer saline cathartics; neutralize alkaloids with tannic acid, together with stimulants.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Privet, Ligustrum, Hedge plant; Ligustrum species; Habitat and Distribution: An ornamental; common as hedge; found at abandoned farm home sites, along fences, and in bottomlands.; Affected Animal(s): Horses; Toxic Parts and Effects: Leaves and fruit. Primarily intestine and stomach irritants. Diarrhea, abdominal pain, incoordination, muscle weakness, weak pulse, fever, convulsions, sometimes death.; Comments and Treatment: Treatment symptomatic and supportive; correct dehydration.

Toxicology / poisoning guidance — Common and Scientific Names: Sorghum, Sudan grass, Kafir, Durra, Milo, Broom-corn, Schrock; Sorghum vulgare; Habitat and Distribution: Forage crops and escapes; throughout North America; Affected Animal(s): All; Toxic Parts and Effects: Heavy in vegetative parts. Short course. Difficult breathing, bloat, staggering, convulsions, death. Blood bright red (cyanide) or chocolate brown (nitrate).; Comments and Treatment: Hay safe for cyanide (volatile), not safe for nitrate (analyze). See also and .
